query: For an equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy made from low-activation refractory elements, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations expected relative to pure tungsten, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Chemical‐disorder–induced spreading of 〈111〉 screw-dislocation cores in the equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy lowers the Peierls barrier by ≳30 % relative to pure W; the reduced lattice friction allows early dislocation glide that (i) provides ≥5-fold larger plastic strain and (ii) enables crack-tip blunting that doubles the high-temperature fracture toughness when both materials are tested at 800 ± 25 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Hot-rolled and recrystallised bar, average grain size 10 ± 2 µm, vacuum-annealed at 1200 °C/2 h to relieve residual stress; equiatomic WTaTiVZr (body-centred cubic solid solution) versus high-purity (>99.97 %) tungsten prepared identically.
generation.intervention: Replace pure W with an equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy solid solution, keeping processing, grain size and surface condition constant.
generation.conditions: Mechanical loading in vacuum (≤10⁻⁵ Pa) at 800 °C (representative of steady-state plasma-facing-component service); strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ for tension and 3-point bending under displacement control for toughness measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Delocalised, compositionally rough 〈111〉 screw‐dislocation cores created by severe local lattice distortion and chemical short-range order.
generation.mechanism: Core delocalisation reduces the Peierls stress, so screw dislocations glide at lower applied stress. Enhanced dislocation mobility gives (a) earlier onset of plastic flow, raising uniform elongation, and (b) increased slip activity ahead of a crack tip, promoting blunting instead of cleavage, thus increasing KᴵC.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to pure W at 800 °C: 1) critical resolved shear stress on {110}〈111〉 slip is lower by ≈30–40 %; 2) tensile yield strength rises from ≈350 MPa (W) to ≈600 MPa (HEA) but uniform elongation increases from ≈2 % to ≥15 %; 3) J-integral fracture toughness increases from ≈15 MPa√m (W) to ≥30 MPa√m (HEA).
generation.baseline: Pure tungsten tested under identical microstructural state and thermal–mechanical conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for 700–1000 °C, grain size ≤50 µm, and single-phase BCC WTaTiVZr. Outside this window (e.g., precipitation of intermetallics or temperatures <600 °C where W itself is brittle) the mechanism or magnitude of benefits may change.
generation.uncertainty: Size of Peierls-stress reduction and exact toughness gain are inferred from analogous multi-principal BCC alloys; no direct data yet exist for equimolar WTaTiVZr.

falsification_experiment.design: 1) Machine 10 µm-diameter [001] micropillars from both alloys; compress at 800 °C to extract CRSS. 2) Conduct isothermal tensile tests and single-edge-notch-bend (SENB) tests at 800 °C on macro-scale specimens of both alloys with matched grain size. All tests in high vacuum.
measurements: Critical resolved shear stress from micropillar yield load
Engineering stress–strain curves (yield strength, uniform elongation)
J-integral or KᴵC from SENB tests
Post-mortem TEM of dislocation cores for spreading width
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if any two of the following hold: a) CRSS of HEA is not ≥25 % lower than that of W, b) uniform elongation of HEA is <5 % or ≤2× that of W, c) measured KᴵC (or J-integral) of HEA is ≤1.2× that of W.
